final.title: Recovering from brittle automation starts with one workflow
final.body:
If an automation has become brittle, don’t start by rebuilding the whole stack. Start with one question: which recurring workflow broke when it failed, and what is that failure costing you in time or mistakes right now?

That turns a vague AI discussion into a bounded business decision. You can compare three paths on one workflow: fix the automation, replace it, or keep it manual for now. For an owner-operator, that is the useful comparison. The build stays technical; the decision stays human.

Then check fit. Is the workflow repetitive, measurable, and stable enough to benefit from automation at all? If not, the right answer may be process cleanup or a clearer manual handoff. Some workflows do not need another layer of scripting. Annoying, but useful.

The practical next step is simple: write down the one workflow, where it fails, and whether AI actually fits before you spend more time rebuilding it. If it does fit, define a small pilot scope and fixed cost only after you approve the direction. Keep human approval on anything involving money movement or other high-risk decisions.

final.title: Start with one workflow when automation turns brittle
final.body:
If an automation gets brittle, don’t start by rebuilding the whole stack. Start with one workflow that failed and ask a narrower question: what is that break costing you now in time, errors, or extra manual work?

That turns a vague “we should do something with AI” discussion into a bounded owner decision. You compare three things on one recurring workflow: keep it manual for now, fix the automation, or replace it with something simpler. For a small business owner, that is usually the real choice. The build stays technical; the decision stays human.

Then check whether the workflow is actually a good candidate. Is it repetitive, measurable, and stable enough to benefit from automation at all? If not, the better fix may be process cleanup or a clearer manual handoff. Not every broken workflow deserves another layer of scripts. Annoying, but true.

The practical next step is simple: write down the one workflow, where it fails, and whether AI fits before you spend time rebuilding it. If it does fit, define a small pilot scope and a fixed price only after the owner approves the direction. Keep database, automation-tool, and API accounts in the customer’s name from the start, as policy and no-lock-in positioning, and keep human approval in place for any money movement or other high-risk decision.
